title: Civil War Medicine: Two Sides of Care
historicalThesis: The Civil War pushed Union and Confederate medical workers to organize care on a larger scale. Both sides dealt with disease, poor medical knowledge, and long recovery times. Different supplies, transport systems, and labor conditions shaped what hospitals could provide. The war helped expand ambulance services, large hospitals, nursing work, and the use of anesthesia, but many advances in modern medicine came later.

intro.name: Introduction
intro.subtitle: Antebellum Baseline, Crisis of Scale & Historical Argument
intro.description: Before the war, many people were treated at home. The sudden need to care for large armies exposed the limits of American medicine.

exhibits.title: Two Armies, One Medical Crisis
exhibits.subtitle: Why the Civil War changed American medical care
body: Before the Civil War, the U.S. Army had a small medical department. Neither side was ready to care for the large number of sick and wounded soldiers. Most Americans had never spent time in a hospital, and medical workers knew far less about infection than doctors do today.

The war forced both armies to expand hospitals, transport patients, and keep better records. Union and Confederate medical teams faced many of the same problems, but their access to supplies, workers, and transportation differed. This museum compares those experiences and asks which wartime changes still matter.
The war did not invent modern medicine. Some practices already existed, and major discoveries came later. Its main impact was making organized medical care a larger part of American life.
exhibits.citation: Dana B. Shoaf, 'How Civil War Medical Developments Affect Us Every Day,' American Battlefield Trust; Maurice S. Albin, 'The Use of Anesthetics during the Civil War, 1861–1865,' Pharmacy in History 42, no. 3/4 (2000): 99–114.

exhibits.title: Why Medicine Struggled in 1861
exhibits.subtitle: Disease, medical training, and hospital conditions
body: At the start of the war, doctors did not understand how germs caused many infections. Training varied, and hospitals often lacked the cleanliness and equipment expected today. Doctors worked with the knowledge available to them, but serious infections remained hard to prevent or treat.

Disease was a bigger threat to soldiers than combat injuries. Crowded camps helped illnesses spread, while large numbers of patients placed pressure on nurses and surgeons. Both armies had to build hospitals and improve sanitation, supply delivery, and patient transport. The Union also received help from groups such as the U.S. Sanitary Commission.
exhibits.citation: American Battlefield Trust, Dana B. Shoaf, 'How Civil War Medical Developments Affect Us Every Day'; National Museum of Civil War Medicine, 'The Story of Satterlee Hospital.'

exhibits.title: Meet the Two Hospitals
exhibits.subtitle: Satterlee in Philadelphia and Chimborazo in Richmond
body: Field hospitals gave care close to battle. General hospitals worked farther away, where patients often stayed for weeks or months. Many used separate wooden wards with windows and ventilation to make crowded buildings easier to manage.

Our North gallery studies Satterlee General Hospital in Philadelphia, led by Dr. Isaac Israel Hayes. Our South gallery studies Chimborazo Hospital in Richmond, led by Dr. James B. McCaw. Both were large, carefully organized hospitals. Their staff and supplies were different, though, and Chimborazo relied heavily on enslaved labor. Comparing the hospitals shows how medical care was shaped by the war around it.
exhibits.citation: National Museum of Civil War Medicine, 'The Story of Satterlee Hospital'; National Park Service, Richmond National Battlefield Park, 'Chimborazo Hospital.'

exhibits.title: Satterlee Hospital in 1864
exhibits.subtitle: A primary-source image of the Union hospital
body: Satterlee opened in West Philadelphia in 1862. Its first major layout had 33 wards and about 2,500 beds spread across 16 acres. The hospital had access to city water, which helped staff handle cooking, cleaning, and patient care. More than 50,000 soldiers passed through Satterlee before it closed in 1865.

This 1864 lithograph shows its separate wards and central buildings. The layout aimed to bring in fresh air and help staff manage different groups of patients. Study the image for details such as ward placement and access routes. It is evidence of how one Union hospital was planned, not a photograph of the inside of its wards.
exhibits.citation: Free Library of Philadelphia, 'Satterlee U.S.A. General Hospital, West Philadelphia' (1864 lithograph), Digital Collections Item pdcp00420; National Museum of Civil War Medicine, 'The Story of Satterlee Hospital.'

exhibits.title: The People Who Ran Satterlee
exhibits.subtitle: Dr. Hayes, Margaret Hamilton, and the Sisters of Charity
body: Dr. Isaac Israel Hayes managed Satterlee, while surgeons and hospital workers treated and supported patients across its wards. Hayes had worked as a ship's surgeon on Arctic expeditions before the war. Running a hospital of this size required planning, supplies, and detailed daily work.

The Sisters of Charity provided experienced nursing care. Margaret Hamilton, one of the sisters, later described how little rest the nurses received when large groups of soldiers arrived. Their work involved clean beds, food, medicines, and comfort. This exhibit shows how a hospital depended on an entire staff, not only doctors.

staffRoles.duties: Chief executive officer of Satterlee Hospital. Oversaw dozens of ward surgeons, enforced sanitation and ventilation regulations, coordinated rail arrivals of wounded soldiers, and managed administrative records,.

staffRoles.role: Sisters of Charity (including Margaret Hamilton & Sister Mary Gonzaga Grace)
staffRoles.duties: Provided disciplined, experienced nursing care across Satterlee's 34+ wards. Supervised diet kitchens, distributed medicines and bandages, comforted dying and recovering soldiers, and maintained strict cleanliness and order.
Civilian physicians and senior medical students from Philadelphia hired under contract to staff individual wards, perform wound dressings, record case histories, and conduct surgical operations.
Non-commissioned officers skilled in compounding pharmaceuticals in the dispensary, maintaining ward registers, and supervising convalescent soldiers who assisted with lighter hospital duties.

transcription.meta: Margaret Hamilton, firsthand nursing recollection, quoted by the National Museum of Civil War Medicine
transcription.quote: we scarcely had time to eat, rest, or sleep.
transcription.note: These are Hamilton's words, reproduced in later historical research. She worked at Satterlee.

exhibits.citation: Michael Mahr, 'The Story of Satterlee Hospital,' National Museum of Civil War Medicine (2022), quoting nurse Margaret Hamilton's firsthand recollection in Mary Gardner Holland, Our Army Nurses.

exhibits.title: John Worrall: A Patient Who Survived
exhibits.subtitle: An Antietam soldier treated at Satterlee
body: Private John Worrall served with the 59th New York Infantry. After he was wounded at Antietam in September 1862, he received treatment at Satterlee. His case appears in the official postwar Medical and Surgical History of the War of the Rebellion.

Worrall recovered and lived through the war. Records also describe a later medical examination in 1869. His story shows how a soldier's care continued long after the battlefield. The account comes from medical records and historians, not from a diary written by Worrall. We should not invent his feelings or words.
exhibits.citation: National Museum of Civil War Medicine, 'The Story of Satterlee Hospital' (https://www.civilwarmed.org/satterlee-hospital/).

exhibits.title: How Chimborazo Worked
exhibits.subtitle: Dr. McCaw and the medical staff in Richmond
body: Chimborazo opened in Richmond in 1861 and grew into one of the largest hospitals in North America. Dr. James B. McCaw managed a complex of nearly 150 buildings. Around 20 to 30 surgeons worked with nurses, attendants, drivers, cooks, and other workers. Most patients came to recover from sickness or injuries after receiving earlier care.

Chimborazo served tens of thousands of patients, even as Confederate transportation and supplies became harder to manage. Enslaved African Americans performed much of the work needed to keep the hospital running. The size of the operation shows both the hospital's organization and the unequal labor system behind it.

staffRoles.role: Commandant & Surgeon-in-Charge: Dr. James B. McCaw
staffRoles.duties: Organized Chimborazo into five divisions, each supervised by a Surgeon-in-Charge. Operated an independent supply system including a hospital bakery, soap factories, icehouses, canal boats, and goat/cattle farms to.

Appointed after the Confederate Congress authorized female hospital matrons in 1862. Supervised special diet kitchens, managed medicinal whiskey stores, oversaw ward cleanliness, and wrote letters for wounded soldiers.
Performed surgeries, dressed wounds, and sought indigenous botanical substitutes from the Confederate laboratory system when imported pharmaceuticals ran low.

staffRoles.role: Enslaved & Free African American Hospital Workers
staffRoles.duties: Formed the indispensable backbone of Chimborazo's daily operation, working as nurses, cooks, laundresses, ambulance drivers, grave diggers, and ward attendants under coercion and impressment.

exhibits.citation: National Park Service, Richmond National Battlefield Park, 'Chimborazo Hospital' (https://www.nps.gov/rich/learn/historyculture/chimborazo.htm).

exhibits.title: Phoebe Pember's Hospital Account
exhibits.subtitle: A firsthand memoir from Chimborazo, published in 1879
body: Phoebe Yates Pember became a matron at Chimborazo in 1862. She supervised food and supplies for patients and often had to defend her authority in a workplace run mainly by men. As the war continued, she struggled to provide enough food and other essentials.

Pember described these experiences in A Southern Woman's Story, published in 1879. Her memoir gives us an inside view of hospital work, but it also reflects her own views and memories years after the war. Read her words alongside other records to understand both what she saw and what she chose to remember.

transcription.meta: Phoebe Yates Pember, A Southern Woman's Story (1879), page 24
transcription.quote: I learned to make requisitions and to use my power.
transcription.note: A direct excerpt from Pember's firsthand memoir, written after the war.

exhibits.citation: Phoebe Yates Pember, A Southern Woman's Story: Life in Confederate Richmond (1879), Project Gutenberg eBook #63870 (https://www.gutenberg.org/files/63870/63870-h/63870-h.htm); National Park Service, 'Chimborazo Hospital.'

exhibits.title: George Ivy Writes Home
exhibits.subtitle: A letter from Chimborazo, January 15, 1864
body: On January 15, 1864, George Ivy wrote to his wife from Chimborazo Hospital's Fourth Division, Ward 6. The letter is held by William & Mary's Special Collections Research Center. Its catalog describes Ivy asking his wife not to sell their land or cow until he returned.

Ivy's letter helps us see the personal side of hospital life. Even while away from home, he was thinking about his family's future. We have verified the catalog description, not a full transcription, so this exhibit does not put made-up words in his mouth. We also have not confirmed what happened to him after the letter.
exhibits.citation: George Ivy Letter, January 15, 1864, SC 00308, Special Collections Research Center, William & Mary Libraries (archival description).

exhibits.title: The Workers Missing from Most Records
exhibits.subtitle: Enslaved people and hospital labor at Chimborazo
body: Chimborazo depended on the work of enslaved African Americans. They helped prepare food, wash clothing, maintain the buildings, move supplies, and care for patients. Many were hired out by enslavers, who received payment for their labor. This was forced work, not ordinary paid employment.

Confederate soldiers who were recovering or unable to fight also worked in hospital wards, along with a smaller number of female matrons. These different workers kept daily care possible. Many enslaved workers left fewer personal records, so the surviving accounts often tell us more about the people in charge than about those doing the work. The exhibit makes that gap visible.
exhibits.citation: National Park Service, Richmond National Battlefield Park, 'Chimborazo Hospital' (https://www.nps.gov/rich/learn/historyculture/chimborazo.htm).

exhibits.title: A New Ambulance System
exhibits.subtitle: General Orders No. 147, August 2, 1862
body: Early in the war, moving wounded soldiers from battle to medical care was often slow and disorganized. Union medical director Jonathan Letterman worked to change this. In August 1862, the Army of the Potomac issued General Orders No. 147, which set rules for a dedicated ambulance corps.

The order placed ambulance teams under clear leadership and gave them regular duties. Medical care could move through nearby aid stations, field hospitals, and general hospitals farther from battle. This system did not appear everywhere at once, and earlier armies had tried related ideas. Letterman's work helped make organized evacuation a lasting part of U.S. military medicine.

transcription.meta: Army of the Potomac, General Orders No. 147, August 2, 1862
transcription.quote: The ambulance corps will be organized on the basis of a captain to each army corps
transcription.note: Direct excerpt from the original order. Open the source link to read the complete regulations.

exhibits.citation: Army of the Potomac, General Orders No. 147, Aug. 2, 1862 (primary source), reproduced by Ohio State University eHistory.

exhibits.title: A Real Union Medical Team
exhibits.subtitle: Surgeons outside their hospital headquarters, Petersburg, August 1864
body: This 1864 photograph shows surgeons of the Third Division, Ninth Army Corps, outside a hospital headquarters tent near Petersburg, Virginia. The sign on the tent identifies the unit. Unlike the figures in our 3D reconstruction, these are real medical workers photographed during the war.

Each part of a wartime medical team had a role. Surgeons examined patients, attendants helped with basic care, and ambulance workers moved people between treatment sites. Study the photograph, then explore the nearby field hospital reconstruction. The reconstruction is based on several historical sources and is not an exact copy of this tent.
exhibits.citation: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, 'Union surgeons of a division at Petersburg, Va., August 1864' (https://www.loc.gov/item/2018666674/).

exhibits.title: Anesthesia: An Important Change
exhibits.subtitle: What doctors already knew and what the war expanded
body: Many people think Civil War surgery was always done without anesthesia. Records show that anesthesia was used in many major wartime operations. It had been introduced before 1861, so the war did not invent it.

Medical historian Maurice S. Albin studied wartime reports and found extensive recorded use. However, much of the surviving data comes from Union records, which limits direct comparisons between the armies. Wartime experience made anesthesia more familiar to American surgeons, while serious problems with infection and patient safety remained. The evidence shows progress without suggesting that Civil War medicine worked like medicine today.
exhibits.citation: Maurice S. Albin, 'The Use of Anesthetics during the Civil War, 1861–1865,' Pharmacy in History 42, no. 3/4 (2000): 99–114.

exhibits.title: What Still Matters Today?
exhibits.subtitle: The Civil War's medical legacy and the changes that came later
body: Ambulance services: Letterman's system showed the value of trained teams, clear responsibilities, and moving patients through different levels of care. Modern emergency services developed later and have many other influences.

Hospitals and nursing: Large wartime hospitals showed how staff, patient records, food, sanitation, and separate wards could work together. Nurses and other workers took on major responsibilities. These experiences helped shape later hospital and nursing systems.

Anesthesia and medical records: Wartime doctors used anesthesia on a large scale and collected more patient information. Their experiences added to medical practice and research. The war did not produce modern anesthesia, germ theory, antiseptic surgery, X-rays, or antibiotics. Most of those scientific advances came later.
The main lesson is how war pushed medical workers to organize care, even when the science of their time was still limited.
exhibits.citation: Dana B. Shoaf, 'How Civil War Medical Developments Affect Us Every Day,' American Battlefield Trust; Maurice S. Albin (2000); Army of the Potomac, General Orders No. 147 (1862).
